# Quick Intro Tips on Getting Started with Julia and Editing MuKumari.jl

This assumes that you've got Julia installed, etc.
* Please use the official Julia docs for that.

## 1. Basic Project Organization

Julia development revolves around **projects**, not individual files.

A Julia project is simply a directory containing:

* a `Project.toml`
* A `Manifest.toml` - generated by the package management system `Pkg.jl`.
  * You shouldn't need to edit this yourself!
* Source files & scripts

The MuKumari project follows a standard and recommended layout:

```text
.
├── Project.toml
├── Manifest.toml
├── src/
├── test/
└── examples/
```

Each directory has a **distinct purpose**. Understanding these roles is essential to working effectively in Julia.


## 2. `src/`

The `src/` directory defines the **MuKumari library itself**.

```text
src/
├── basic_geometry.jl
├── basic_objectives.jl
├── basic_sim.jl
├── basic_viz.jl
├── intentional_agent.jl
├── intentional_agent_pomdp.jl
├── intentional_kworld.jl
└── MuKumari.jl
```

### 2.1 The Role of `MuKumari.jl`

`MuKumari.jl` defines the module and controls how the library is assembled.

Typical pattern:

```julia
module MuKumari

include("basic_geometry.jl")
include("basic_sim.jl")
include("intentional_agent.jl")

export some_function

end
```

This file:

* defines the module namespace
* pulls in implementation files
* controls what users see via `export`

Users load the library with:

```julia
using MuKumari
```

They can now directly call the function `some_function` within the REPL, as it has been added to the namespace. If they instead run `import MuKumari`, then they can call the function with `MuKumari.some_function`.

### 2.2 The `include(...)` Pattern for Module Development

In Julia, **modules are assembled using `include`**.

Important points:

* `include("file.jl")` evaluates the file *inside the current module*
* Included files do **not** *automatically* define their own modules
  * It is possible an included file adds a sub-module. Do that at your own peril.
* All functions and types become part of `MuKumari`

Example (`basic_geometry.jl`):

```julia
# Not an actually defined function within MuKumari!
function distance(p1, p2)
    return norm(p1 .- p2)
end
```

After inclusion, this function would be available as:

```julia
MuKumari.distance
```

If you wanted to export this as a part of the module's functions, you can do either of the following:

 
1. Export the function in the main `MuKumari.jl` module file, *after* including the source file where the function is defined (in this example, `basic_geometry.jl`). 
```julia
module MuKumari

include("basic_geometry.jl")
include("basic_sim.jl")
include("intentional_agent.jl")

export some_function, distance

end
```

2. Or, export the function directly within the same file where it is defined. Then, it is automatically exported when the source file is included into the main module file.
```julia
# basic_geometry.jl

export distance

# Not an actually defined function within MuKumari!
function distance(p1, p2)
    return norm(p1 .- p2)
end
```

**Best practices:**

* Compose modules by using `include` to load files defined inside `src/` into the main module file
* Do not use `include` to load library code into *external* scripts
  * There are better ways of utilizing library code!
  * Namely, always load the library with `using MuKumari`


## 3. Activating the Project Environment (Always Step One)

Before running *any* code, activate the correct project.

From the project root:

```bash
julia --project=.
```

Or inside Julia:

```julia
] activate .
```

This ensures:

* dependencies are available
* `using MuKumari` works correctly
* Julia resolves packages properly

Not doing this often results in weird package issues, where versions don't seem to resolve or packages can't be loaded or conflict with each other.
* If you're using VS Code as your IDE (_**highly recommended**_), then you can do this by first specifying your Julia environment (`Julia: Change Current Environment`), and then running the command `Julia: Start REPL`. 


## 4. Writing and Running Scripts in `test/`

The `test/` directory is where you **use and validate** the library.

```text
test/
├── runtests.jl
├── single_agent_demo.jl
├── multi_agent_demo.jl
├── multi_agent_experience_generator.jl
├── expert_data/
└── Project.toml
```

### 4.1 Automated Tests (`runtests.jl`)

This file is executed when you run:

```julia
] test
```

It should contain:

* `using Test`
* `@testset` blocks
* automated correctness checks only

I didn't use this method when writing `MuKumari.jl`, mainly because I am not skilled with using test cases. Instead, I use the manual script option to trial various aspects of my library code, using the second method mentioned below.

### 4.2 Manual Scripts, Demos, and Exploration

Files such as:

```text
single_agent_demo.jl
multi_agent_demo.jl
```

are **scripts**, not formal tests.

They are used to:

* run simulations
* generate plots
* load saved data
* explore behavior interactively

Typical script pattern:

```julia
using MuKumari

# Do some trial work leveraging functions from MuKumari
stepthrough_sim(...)
```

#### Running a script from the command line

```bash
julia --project=. test/single_agent_demo.jl
```

#### Running a script from the REPL

```julia
include("test/single_agent_demo.jl")
```

Think of `include` here as:

> “Execute this file right now.”


### Iterative Development with `Revise` and `includet`

When experimenting repeatedly, you can use `Revise.jl`:

```julia
using Revise
includet("test/single_agent_demo.jl")
```

This allows you to:

* edit the script
* re-run functions
* avoid restarting the REPL
  * This applies when either MuKumari has been changed or the script! But,
  * This no longer applies when static object definitions have been changed. For example, if the definition of an immutable `struct` has changed, then you'll have to reload the REPL anyways.

**Important distinction:**

* `include` is appropriate for scripts
* library code must be loaded via `using MuKumari`, not `include`


### Test-Specific Dependencies

Sometimes (actually, a lot of times), you'll want to use additional packages during testing that are irrelevant to the main project. There are a few ways to do this - using `test` flags when adding a package to the environment, and so on - but I prefer to just create a separate project environment within the `test/` directory. This means the `test/` directory contains its own `Project.toml`.

This allows:

* plotting
* profiling
* Python interop
* large datasets

without affecting the main library dependencies.

Activate it explicitly if needed:

```julia
] activate test
```

Equivalently, you can run `Julia: Change Current Environment` in VS Code and navigate to the `test/` folder. This will establish the `test/` folder as the parent directory for the project.


## 5. Example Projects (`examples/`)

The `examples/` directory contains **standalone Julia projects** that provide use-cases of how to use `MuKumari.jl` in actual projects (hence the folder title `examples/`).

```text
examples/
├── single_trace_inference/
│   ├── Project.toml
│   ├── inf_on_single_trace.jl
│   ├── particle_trial.jl
│   └── data files
└── multi_trace_inference/
    ├── Project.toml
    └── inf_multi_trace.jl
```

Each subdirectory:

* is a fully independent project
* has its own dependencies
* demonstrates real usage of MuKumari

This is the recommended way to distribute reproducible examples.

---

## 6. Using MuKumari from an Example Project

### Step 1: Activate the example project

```bash
cd examples/single_trace_inference
julia --project=.
```

Or use the VS Code command `Julia: Change Current Environment`. In this case (and honestly in general), it's best that you start the Julia session/REPL in the package environment that you will use, rather than opening a Julia session and then navigating to the right project environment via `;cd /path/to/right/project` and `]activate .`

### Step 2: Add the local MuKumari package

```julia
] dev /absolute/path/to/MuKumari.jl
```

This tells Julia:

> “Use my local working copy of MuKumari.”

Edits to `src/` now apply immediately.

### Step 3: Use it normally like you would any other package

```julia
using MuKumari
```

### Running example scripts

After opening a REPL in the right project (assuming `single_trace_inference` for this example):
```julia
include("fft_synth.jl")
```
Be careful that occasionally VS Code will start a REPL with the right project environment but decide the REPL is still running in the `MuKumari.jl` root folder. (Meaning that you'll need to run `include("examples/single_trace_inference/fft_synth.jl")` instead.)

Or, if you want to run it from a command line (assuming you're already at the `MuKumari.jl` project root):
```bash
julia --project=examples/single_trace_inference \
      examples/single_trace_inference/inf_on_single_trace.jl
```

## 7. Recommended Daily Development Workflow

1. Start Julia REPL in the right project for what you're working on
4. Include scripts interactively (`includet()`)
5. Use scripts in `test/` for validation of library code
6. Use `examples/` for reproducible demonstrations of library use-cases.
